quote: Wie fin- det man ein Maass zur Beurteilung für die Genau- igkeit des Erfülltsein's der Axiome? doch wohl immer nur, indem man gewisse Axiome als genau oder fast genau erfüllt ansieht!
english: How does one find a measure for judging the accuracy with which the axioms are fulfilled? Surely always only by regarding certain axioms as exactly or almost exactly fulfilled!
topic: Brief philosophical notes on how accurately the axioms of geometry hold empirically, on theories needing a point, on mathematical existence as freedom from contradiction (with examples of algebraic roots and surfaces of negative curvature), and on Lilienthal's flights refuting Helmholtz's claim about the maximum mass of flying birds.

triage.modern_statement: This isn't a mathematical research question. It's an epistemological remark about applying geometry to physical space. Put in modern terms: if we test whether the axioms of geometry hold empirically (for example, whether a measured triangle's angles add up to 180°, or whether congruence and parallel axioms hold for rigid bodies and light rays), how do we measure how far they fail? Hilbert's own answer is that you can only do it by assuming some other axioms hold exactly or nearly exactly, such as those used to define measuring rods, straight lines or congruence. So any empirical test of one axiom depends on others. In philosophy of science this is the issue of conventionalism and confirmation holism (Poincaré, Duhem–Quine), and it belongs to Hilbert's empiricist view of geometry as a natural science, which led to his 6th Problem on axiomatizing physics.
triage.answered_by: There is no mathematical answer because it isn't a mathematical problem. The point was taken up in philosophy of science: Poincaré's conventionalism held that the axioms of geometry can't be disconfirmed by experiment alone, and the Duhem–Quine thesis says hypotheses can't be tested in isolation. In Hilbert's own work the theme fed into his lectures on the foundations of geometry (1891–1902, edited by Hallett & Majer in 2004) and into the 6th of his 1900 problems, on axiomatizing physics. evidence.claim: Poincaré argued that geometry can't be tested empirically, because any such test happens inside physics, which already presupposes the principles of geometry. On this view the Euclidean axioms are conventions that experiment cannot disconfirm.
Poincaré held that geometry is a convention and can't be tested experimentally. Einstein's view on the testability of geometry was the counterpart in this debate.

The Duhem–Quine thesis says a scientific hypothesis can't be falsified unambiguously on its own, because tests always rely on auxiliary assumptions. This is the general form of Hilbert's point that judging one axiom means taking others as exact.
Hilbert's 6th Problem grew out of his work on the foundations of geometry and its links to the empirical sciences, reflecting his empiricist approach to axiomatization (1894–1932).
Hilbert's lectures on the foundations of geometry from 1891–1902, where he discussed geometry as an empirical science, were published by Hallett and Majer (2004).
